Given a question and an answer, analyze the complexity of each sentence in the answer. Break down each sentence into one or more fully understandable statements. Ensure that no pronouns are used in any statement. Format the outputs in JSON.
Please return the output in a JSON format that complies with the following schema as specified in JSON Schema:
{"properties": {"statements": {"description": "The generated statements", "items": {"type": "string"}, "title": "Statements", "type": "array"}}, "required": ["statements"], "title": "StatementGeneratorOutput", "type": "object"}Do not use single quotes in your response but double quotes,properly escaped with a backslash.

--------EXAMPLES-----------
Example 1
Input: {
    "question": "Who was Albert Einstein and what is he best known for?",
    "answer": "He was a German-born theoretical physicist, widely acknowledged to be one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time. He was best known for developing the theory of relativity, he also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics."
}
Output: {
    "statements": [
        "Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist.",
        "Albert Einstein is recognized as one of the greatest and most influential physicists of all time.",
        "Albert Einstein was best known for developing the theory of relativity.",
        "Albert Einstein also made important contributions to the development of the theory of quantum mechanics."
    ]
}
-----------------------------

Now perform the same with the following input
input: {
    "question": "user: Are all financial advisors compensated in the same way?\nassistant: Not all financial advisors are compensated in the same way. Some financial advisors are compensated based on transactions, which can create a conflict of interest as they may have a vested interest to churn your account. Others collect an annual fee based on a percentage of your account value, which can be a better option. Some announce that they are fee-based - these advisers often receive fees as well as commissions. Some advisors may also receive commissions for selling certain products, like mutual funds with sales loads or annuities. Therefore, it's important to understand your advisor's compensation structure to ensure their interests align with yours.\nuser: How much does a fee only Financial Advisor charge?\nassistant: You are better served by an advisor who collects an annual fee based on a percentage of your account value. Be suspicious of an advisor with a 1% fee. My advisor charges a monthly fee of $50, but also gets a percentage based portion of certain investments, based on a $150/hr rate that amounts to 4 hrs/yr. Make sure you have a \"fee only\" advisor who is not connected to a company which sells financial products. Your advisor's compensation structure should be transparent. Check Investopedia for choosing a financial advisor.\nuser: Is there a cheaper option?\nassistant: Robo-advisers are fairly new. They often don't allow you to pick individual holdings, so these services are best when you want to passively invest. If it supports your 401k plan, you can use FutureAdvisor. The fee is $39/yr, with a free trial. But there are many other robo-advisor start-ups: Betterment, Wealthfront, Personal Capital, Sigfig and Robinhood. Since they haven't been around that long, it's hard to tell how effective these are and whether they beat the market.\nuser: Are robo-advisors insured by FDIC?\nassistant: No, robo-advisors are not insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). FDIC insurance only protects certain funds (savings, checking, money market and CDs), and is not meant to protect against losses in the market. A protection similar to FDIC for banks is provided to brokerage accounts' owners by SIPC. Your investment losses are obviously not insured. FDIC and SIPC only provide protection for bank/brokerage failures.\nuser: What about investing with Lendingclub or Prosper?",
    "answer": "According to page 1, one contributor invested in both Prosper and Lending Club and reported better returns with Lending Club. After 18 months, they reported returns of 4–5% on Prosper and 11–12% on Lending Club, describing both investments as satisfactory. They attributed Lending Club’s better performance to stronger underwriting standards, but this was their opinion, not an established finding.\n\nThis is an individual’s experience, not enough evidence to determine whether either platform is suitable for you or what returns you could expect. The document provides no further information about their risks, fees, or investor protections."
}
